title: Executive summary - every service, its verbs and its MCP cover
intro: One row per IDMC service. The verbs column is what has actually been proven to work; the quirk column is the thing about that service's verb behaviour that will trip you up; the MCP column says whether any MCP server reaches this service at all.

rows: Users, groups, roles, schedules, metering, audit. v3 objects is GET-only.
Clone-only. A hand-built package is always rejected.
no PUT anywhere; POST /{id} is the update
Run, schedule, connect, monitor. Mapping design is canvas-only.
Bulk publish and unpublish, max 199 assets.
URN uses PUT for add AND update
The richest runtime-control plane: suspend, resume, terminate, schedule.
Scan and search are scriptable. Glossary, classification accept and lineage are not.
NO GET ANYWHERE in the API
Dictionaries are write-only. Rule logic and scoring are UI.
Rich read of profiles, metrics and patterns.
Engines running; authoring is a wizard. Not a licence gap.
Broadest verb coverage in the governance family.
the ONLY service where PATCH matters
Record ingest works. Business-entity deploy has no verb.
Two resources. One active request per org, no pagination.

notes.label: Read the MCP column first if you are choosing an interface.
notes.text: Only five of the thirteen services have any MCP coverage at all, and every MCP action is an HTTP POST regardless of what it does - the read-or-write intent lives in the action name. So MCP is not a verb-level alternative to REST; it is a small curated subset with two capabilities REST lacks.

notes.label: Two verb quirks that hold across the whole platform.
notes.text: The v2 plane has almost no PUT - you POST to /api/v2/<resource>/{id} to update, so an absent PUT is usually correct behaviour rather than a gap. And PATCH is only meaningful in MDM; elsewhere it is 405 or undefined.
